explain.narrative:
## Java Optional

Optional represents a value that may be absent and is most useful as a method return type. Use map and filter, and orElseGet for lazy fallback calculation.

Identify the input and desired result. Select the Java construct or API that supports the requirement. Keep code readable, handle documented failures and state assumptions clearly.

Compile with JDK 21, predict output before running, and test normal, boundary and invalid inputs.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.of("Java"); System.out.println(value.orElse("none")); } }
examples.explanation: An Optional containing a value returns it.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.empty(); System.out.println(value.orElse("fallback")); } }
examples.explanation: An empty Optional uses the fallback value.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.of("java"); System.out.println(value.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("none")); } }

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<Integer> value = java.util.Optional.of(5); System.out.println(value.filter(n -> n > 3).isPresent()); } }
examples.explanation: filter retains the value when its predicate matches.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.ofNullable(null); System.out.println(value.isEmpty()); } }
examples.explanation: ofNullable safely represents a possibly null result.
